title: Thermal avalanches in a quasiperiodic XXZ model
abstract: We study bath-induced thermalization in the many-body localized XXZ spin chain subjected to a quasiperiodic magnetic field. We engineer a thermal inclusion by setting the field strength in one part of the chain below the localization threshold and analyze thermalization via the avalanche mechanism. To study the nature of such avalanches, we use two complementary observables, namely the two-point connected correlation function and the particle-number entropy. Surprisingly, the correlations alone show no signatures of avalanches. Instead, they display a logarithmic growth of the correlation length throughout the dynamics and predict localization lengths of the local integrals of motion that remain well below the avalanche threshold. In contrast, the particle number entropy shows clear signatures of the thermal avalanche, with the avalanche front progressively propagating deeper into the localized subsystem for sufficiently large baths. The discrepancy between the two observables shows that two-point correlations are unreliable in identifying thermal avalanches in quasiperiodic systems, as opposed to the random case. On one hand, qualitative results are consistent with the analytical predictions of the standard avalanche theory. On the other hand, significant quantitative deviations persist, which could be due to short-range resonances generated by the quasiperiodic potential. Our results suggest that the standard avalanche framework requires revision to account for the short-range correlations of quasiperiodic potentials.
summary: The paper examines how heat spreads (thermalizes) in a localized spin chain coupled to an external bath under quasiperiodic driving. By comparing two diagnostics—correlations and entropy—the authors find that only the entropy reveals clear signs of thermal avalanches, while correlations do not. This suggests that standard theories describing such spreading must be updated to account for the unique short-range physics introduced by quasiperiodicity.
main_problem: The study investigates bath-induced thermalization, specifically analyzing the mechanism of 'thermal avalanches' in a Many-Body Localized (MBL) system subjected to a quasiperiodic magnetic field.
main_result: The particle-number entropy clearly shows signatures of thermal avalanches propagating into the localized subsystem, whereas two-point correlations fail to show this signature, suggesting standard avalanche theory needs revision for quasiperiodic potentials.
method: The analysis uses quantum simulation techniques by comparing results from two complementary observables: the two-point connected correlation function and the particle-number entropy, within an XXZ spin chain model.
model_or_system: The system is an XXZ spin chain partitioned into a localized subsystem (A) coupled to a thermal bath (B), subjected to both interacting and quasiperiodic magnetic fields. The dynamics are analyzed by engineering a thermal inclusion in the bath region.
key_observables: Two-point connected correlation function, particle-number entropy, correlation length ($\xi_d(t)$), and entanglement entropy ($S_E$).
important_parameters: Quasiperiodic field strength ($W_A$), weak disorder in the bath ($W_B=0.5$), and the comparison between quasiperiodic vs. random potentials.
main_assumptions: The standard avalanche theory framework is assumed to apply, but the authors argue this assumption breaks down due to short-range correlations inherent to quasiperiodic potentials.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates thermal bubble spreading, showing the localized subsystem A coupled to an ergodic bath B, with a red curve indicating the propagating thermalization front.
paper_structure: The paper sets up the MBL system under external fields, introduces two diagnostic observables (correlations and entropy), compares their predictions regarding avalanche signatures, and concludes by proposing necessary revisions to existing theoretical frameworks based on the observed discrepancy.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium quantum dynamics in quasiperiodic systems, a key area intersecting MBL physics with open quantum system theory. The finding that different observables yield conflicting results highlights the need for careful diagnostic tools when modeling complex many-body thermalization processes.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Thermal bubble spreading in a quasiperi- odic spin chain. A localized subsystem A (blue, quasiperi- odic amplitude WA) is coupled to an ergodic bath B (red, quasiperiodic amplitude WB). The bath acts as a seed for thermalization, generating after time tB a thermal bubble that gradually invades subsystem A. The red curve indicates the position of the thermalization front, which propagates ap- proximately logarithmically in time.

FIG. 2. Two-point connected correlation function. Logarithm of sample-averaged two-point correlations at short, t = 1 (a), and long times t = 10000 (b-d). The potential strength in the subsytem A is (a),(d) WA = 10, (b) W = 1.5, and (c) W = 3.0. The times are in units of the hopping J. In all plots, we used chains with L = 16 sites and the bath con- taining LB = 8 sites with weak potential strength WB = 0.5. The dynamics is calculated starting from an initial N´eel state. Dashed yellow lines enclose the sites belonging to the bath.

FIG. 3. Bath-averaged two-point correlation function and bath thermalization. (a) Mean of the off-diagonal elements of g(2) calculated only in the bath region, i.e. i, j ∈ LB, for three different strengths of the potential. (b) Bath- averaged g(2) as a function of the distance from the bath i plotted for three different hopping times. Dashed color-coded lines show the exponential fit inside the localized part of the system. The vertical dashed line shows the position of the last site in the localized subsystem, i.e. i = LA. For all curves we used L = 16, LA = 8, and WA = 3.0, WB = 0.5. All parameters, except WA, are the same as in (a).

FIG. 4. Time dynamics of the correlation length. Correlation length ξd as a function of time for different WA for (a)-(b) a large bath with L = 16, LB = 8, (c)-(d) a small bath with L = 16, LB = 2. The dashed lines in (a) and (c) show the exponential fit, from which the LIOM localization length ξ is extracted in (b) and (d).
